layer1: a tracker migration: the old tracker's Bugzilla-style CSV export (product and component as two columns, Helsinki local timestamps, resolution codes, a dupe_of column) against the new tracker's Jira-style JSON export (component paths, UTC timestamps, a duplicate link type)

the triage dashboard's weekly totals per product area on the old counting basis (duplicates not counted, Monday-to-Sunday weeks in Helsinki time) against the new tracker's basis (every report a triage item, duplicates included)
the four-week November parallel run in both trackers, with the old dashboard and the new tracker counting the same reports differently
the public bug statistics, which leave out security-restricted reports, beside the internal export, which holds them
a product-area reorganisation in 2025 (one area split in two, components moved) mapped by the area register
the public statistics' daily version adoption by platform in its own layout (shares of daily active installs, not counts)
driver: A unit takes up each new version only at its next restart, and on the dominant platform most restarts come in a two-day burst once a month on a fixed day, so the share of units that reach a version in its first week, and the reports that follow their first use, are set by whether the burst falls inside that week; every version in the forward window ships on the burst's eve, which no version in the last year did, so the record's first-week profile, its busiest weeks or a ratio taken from the last version all understate each forward release week, and only the version-by-version restart model the record supports, ordinary restarts plus the monthly burst, sets them.
driver_concrete: The browser's update is applied when the browser restarts, and most Windows machines restart in the two days after Microsoft's Patch Tuesday, so a release that ships a week or two before or after Patch Tuesday reaches users through ordinary restarts first and meets the Windows burst later, while a release shipped on Patch Tuesday meets the burst in its own first week; every release since autumn 2025 shipped off Patch Tuesday, and all three of the first quarter's releases ship on it, so their release weeks reach about one and a half times the usual share of users and carry the first-use reports and duplicates that follow, putting the busiest week at about 900 triage items.
stump: Rebuilding the new tracker's weekly triage items from the old export and carrying the record's release-week profile, or the busiest week of the past year scaled for growth, onto the first quarter files 7 triagers; the step that lands it there is treating each first-quarter release week as typical, when all three releases ship on Patch Tuesday, so the Windows restart burst that the past year's releases met a week or two after release falls inside each release week, and the busiest week (8 to 14 March) carries about 900 items and needs 8.
analyst_test: A strong analyst who rebuilds the new tracker's items from the old export (every report, duplicates included), reads the counting basis, the 120-item standard and the release calendar correctly, and forecasts the quarter with trend, seasonality and the record's release-week profile, or scales the past year's busiest week for growth, files 7 triagers; only modelling each release's adoption as ordinary restarts plus the monthly Windows restart burst after Patch Tuesday, which the public adoption series shows month after month, and placing all three first-quarter releases on Patch Tuesday files 8.
domain_test: The deciding quantity is each release week's first-use report wave, forecast the way product analytics forecasts version-driven activity: from the version's adoption curve (the update applies at the next browser restart, and on Windows most restarts come in the two days after Patch Tuesday) carried through the reports users file in their first days on the version; with a hospital's patients or a utility's megawatt-hours there is no update applied at restart and no operating-system restart cycle deciding when users reach a new version, so the quantity that decides the call has nothing to stand on.

differentiation.task156: task156 sizes paid moderators from the work a shrinking volunteer pool cannot absorb, capacity seen only where it fell short; here no capacity is censored and no pool shrinks: the triage load is a demand forecast whose release weeks are set by when users reach each new version, and the decisive quantity is the share of users a release reaches in its first week.
differentiation.task160: task160 times regional surge waves by a stable propagation lag behind the region the wave starts in, observed this season; here nothing propagates: an external monthly restart cycle fixed by the operating system's calendar decides when each release reaches its users, and the forward releases' position in that cycle is known from the release calendar, not read from this season's wave.
differentiation.task161: task161 draws down a stock built ahead of a cost step at each holder's own use share; here there is no stock or drawdown: each release's reach in its first week is set by an external monthly restart burst, and the forecast is of first-use reports.
differentiation.task157: task157 completes a returning cohort's wave from the part already back at the as-of; here no wave is in flight at the as-of: the forward releases are not yet shipped, and their first-week reach comes from where each sits in the monthly restart cycle.
differentiation.task148: task148 drains a queue by abandonment; here no queue or patience enters: the forecast is of arrivals.
differentiation.task159: task159 builds a backlog where services arrive with less room than one interval's arrivals; here arrivals are forecast and no service capacity censors them.
differentiation.task102: task102 recovers a next-business-day release rule from the payment history and applies it to a forward period that ends on a weekend; here no rule is recovered and no period boundary moves anything: an adoption process (each install updates at its next restart, Windows restarts bunched in the two days after Patch Tuesday) is estimated from the public adoption series across every release, and the forward releases' place in the monthly cycle sets how many users each reaches in its first week.
differentiation.task130: task130 prices a short cover window from past events by how soon each was reported; here there is no cover window and no reporting delay to price: the forecast is of the first-use reports that follow each release's adoption, set by when its users restart.
differentiation.task134: task134's second architecture scaled an announced threshold step from the one smaller step its history held; here nothing is announced and nothing is scaled from one event: the restart burst recurs every month in the adoption record and every release since 2023 met it at some point of its first month.
differentiation.task501: task501's third architecture read a facility buffer off the furthest a cumulative path ran ahead of its forecast; here the quantity is one week's first-use reports, set by where each release sits in the monthly restart cycle, and no buffer, path or validation error is graded.
